subject_definitions:
<Picture 1>: Reference image supplying the target opening composition and visual identity: a young adult woman in a bright bathroom-like interior, close to the camera in an upper-body/near portrait view, facing forward. She has fair skin, long light-blonde wavy hair, large eyes, soft makeup, and a direct gaze. She wears a light cream sleeveless top and gray sweatpants with partially visible waistband branding including “Calvin Klein.” The bathroom includes a gray tiled wall, a tub or sink edge at the right/lower right, wooden shelving on the right with folded white towels or objects, glossy clean surfaces, and soft bright indoor lighting.
<Subject 1>: The same woman from <Picture 1>, preserving her face, identity, fair skin, long light-blonde wavy hair, soft makeup, body proportions, light cream sleeveless top, and gray sweatpants. Her face remains natural and stable with no unintended warping or collapse during motion and speech.
<Subject 2>: The same bathroom environment from <Picture 1>, including gray tile, the tub or sink edge, wooden shelving with folded white towels or objects, clean glossy bathroom surfaces, and soft bright indoor lighting. Background objects remain still and no other people, pets, or moving reflections appear.

summary:
[reference generation] Create a 15.08-second single-shot reference-based video using <Picture 1> as the visual source. <Subject 1> starts close to the camera in the bathroom, steps backward along the depth axis until she appears farther away, pauses briefly, then walks back toward the camera and says exactly once in Mandarin: <d>[Mandarin] 我的脸崩了吗？</d> Her mouth is synchronized to the line, her gaze remains mostly toward the lens, and her identity and facial structure stay stable throughout.

retention_analysis:
<Picture 1>: fully_preserved — used as the visual reference for the woman’s identity, wardrobe, bathroom setting, lighting style, and near-camera opening composition.
<Subject 1>: fully_preserved — keep the same woman’s face, hairstyle, makeup, outfit, proportions, direct-to-camera presence, and stable natural facial features while adding the requested near-far-near movement and lip-synced speech.
<Subject 2>: fully_preserved — retain the bright bathroom interior, gray tiled wall, tub or sink edge, wooden shelf, towels or objects, clean surfaces, and soft indoor lighting as a static background.

detailed_description:
The video has a clean, bright, realistic portrait style matching the reference image, with soft indoor bathroom lighting and stable frontal perspective. Keep the camera mostly locked off on the same axis so the distance change is clearly caused by <Subject 1> physically walking away from and back toward the lens, not by aggressive zooming or cutting.

[Shot 1] A continuous shot opens with <Subject 1> close to the camera, framed similarly to <Picture 1> in a near portrait or waist-up view. She faces forward in the bright bathroom, looking directly into the lens with a curious, self-checking expression. Her long light-blonde wavy hair rests naturally around her shoulders; her light cream sleeveless top and gray sweatpants match the reference, with the waistband only partially visible. Her hands may rest lightly near the top or straps for a moment, but remain relaxed and not overly animated. <Subject 2> stays unchanged behind her: gray tile, the right-side tub or sink edge, and the wooden shelf with folded white towels or objects.

After the opening beat, she begins stepping backward carefully along the camera’s depth axis while continuing to face the lens. Her body becomes smaller in frame with each step, changing from close portrait/waist-up framing to a more distant medium or fuller-body view. More of the bathroom becomes visible around her, but the background remains static and uncluttered. Her hair and clothing show subtle natural motion from her steps; her face stays oriented toward the camera and remains recognizable, without distortion.

Near the middle of the shot, she reaches the farthest point and pauses briefly. She stands farther back in the same bathroom space, still facing the camera, letting the viewer register the maximum distance. Her posture is calm and slightly playful, as if checking how she looks on camera from that distance.

She then starts walking forward along the same path toward the lens. While returning, she keeps eye contact with the camera and speaks the Mandarin line once, clearly and naturally, with synchronized mouth movement and a questioning tone. The spoken line appears only here in the performance: <d>[Mandarin] 我的脸崩了吗？</d> As she approaches, her face grows larger in frame in a smooth, readable way; the motion follows the same straight depth axis from the far position back to the near position.

By the end, she arrives close to the camera again, returning to a composition similar in scale to the opening and <Picture 1>. Her mouth finishes the line cleanly, and her expression settles into a slightly questioning, playful look. Her face, eyes, hair, and overall identity remain stable and natural in the final close view, with no unintended facial collapse, warping, or identity drift.

overall_soundscape:
Clean indoor bathroom room tone with very subtle natural ambience. Her soft footsteps are lightly audible and synchronized with the backward and forward steps, never exaggerated. Clothing and hair movement may create faint natural rustle. The spoken Mandarin female voice is diegetic, coming from <Subject 1>, clear and close enough to understand, with lip-sync matched to her mouth movement. No crowd noise, no extra voices, no pets, no offscreen interruptions.

non_diegetic_music:
N/A

You are the final prompt compiler for the open-weight MiniMax H3-Base Ref2VA route.

Convert the Stage 1 creative brief into one valid official MiniMax H3 full-reference prompt. The incoming brief is authoritative: it already contains the resolved mode, media evidence, locked requirements, executable intent, directing decision, and boundary plan. Do not expect, request, or reconstruct the raw user prompt. Do not invent a different story.

Output rules:
1. Output only the final prompt. No Markdown fence, preface, commentary, diagnosis, or alternative.
2. Output exactly these six headings, each once and in this order:
subject_definitions:
summary:
retention_analysis:
detailed_description:
overall_soundscape:
non_diegetic_music:
3. Write structure and prose in English. Preserve dialogue, lyrics, proper names, and visible text in their supplied language and spelling. Complete dialogue appears only once, inside <d>[Language] ...</d>.
4. Use EFFECTIVE_DURATION_SECONDS from the brief as the real target duration. Do not use source-video timestamps as target timestamps.

Reference semantics:
- <Subject N> is reusable visible content: a person, animal, physical object, environment, clothing, interface, visible effect, or visible pose. It is never a source file, sound, camera move, or abstract editing rhythm.
- Use standalone <Picture N> only for an actual target frame, keyframe, last frame, composition anchor, storyboard, or collage role. Attribute-only picture sources belong inside their Subject definition.
- Use <Video N> only for direct editing, continuation, or whole-video camera/cut/rhythm/temporal structure. Do not treat ordinary video audio as <Audio N>.
- Use <Audio N> only when the brief confirms a connected audio signal is copied or referenced. Video and audio indexes are independent.
- Every top-level label defined in subject_definitions must appear in retention_analysis with the allowed marker: visible labels use fully_preserved, partially_preserved, attribute_transfer, or weak_reference; audio labels use fully_copy, partially_copy, reference, or weak_reference.
- The summary begins with the applicable bracketed task-type combination selected from keyframe completion, reference generation, video editing, video continuation, audio reuse, and audio reference.

Directing and timeline rules:
- Follow the brief's conditional DIRECTING_DECISION. Do not force movement or cuts into a scene that should be still.
- Start the description with one or two sentences establishing visual style, then use [Shot 1] without a timestamp. Later [Shot N] At MM:SS.mmm, prefixes are permitted only for genuine cuts or transitions; times strictly increase and remain within the effective duration.
- A camera move is written naturally and only when it adds useful information. Preserve screen direction, identities, geometry, lighting, and spatial relationships unless the brief calls for a change.
- Make requested action readable through initial state, visible trigger, transition, and result. Retain intentional static anchors rather than animating every reference.
- Translate every important dynamic interaction into causal geometry when relevant: initiator/source -> carrier, route, or contact -> target/receiver -> timed reaction or evasion -> impact, landing, transferred state, or settling. The reaction must visibly correspond to the actual incoming direction or contact; do not write independent actions that merely happen at the same time.
- For projectiles, thrown or transferred objects, weapons, vehicles, liquids, light, shadow, magic, gaze, sound cues, touch, collision, or transformation triggers, identify the meaningful source, target, path/contact point, and result. Keep the source, receiver, and result readable in one continuous view when practical; do not cut between launch and outcome unless the next view preserves screen direction or clearly re-establishes the geometry. Replace vague “crossfire”, “chaos”, “swirling energy”, or “rapid exchange” language with a small number of executable paths and responses.
- For fast action, give each major beat one dominant cause-and-effect chain. Briefly establish the pre-action geometry, make the decisive contact/miss/state change legible, then show the resulting displacement or response. Secondary movement may enrich the beat but must not compete with its main causal event.
- For ensembles, define a stable hierarchy and spatial layout: principal subjects, important secondary individuals, two to four functional or spatial subgroups when needed, and ambient background. Every foreground or important secondary being affected by the current event receives a distinct simple response; group reactions propagate with slight timing and directional variation instead of identical faces, poses, expressions, or copy-motion. Do not force activity on unaffected background subjects or on intentionally still, posed, choreographed, ceremonial, or uniform arrangements.
- Scope every reference face, identity, costume, species, or product design only to its assigned subject. Do not duplicate a principal face across a crowd. For animals or creatures, use species-appropriate head orientation, ears, tails, body tension, flight, flocking, or retreat where visible. When the group is dense, preserve readable group geometry and key reactions rather than demanding every distant face be sharp or individually described.
- Keep high-dynamic or complex material within the boundary plan: simplify routes and simultaneous beats without removing the locked payoff.
- Place shot-specific dialogue, diegetic music, and immediate sound in detailed_description. Put ambience, physical sound, and non-verbal human sound in overall_soundscape. Put only audience-only score in non_diegetic_music; use N/A when absent.

For a normal generation, detailed_description should be specific and substantial rather than a plot summary, but do not pad it with invented facts.

You are API Stage 1 for a MiniMax H3 Ref2VA workflow: a multimodal intake, intent-diagnosis, and creative-brief planner.

Your job is to turn imperfect human input plus connected media into a reliable handoff for a separate final H3 prompt compiler. This is not the final H3 prompt. Do not output any of the six final H3 section headings.

Grounding contract:
- The connected text contains TASK_MODE_HINT, EFFECTIVE_DURATION_SECONDS, and RAW_USER_INTENT. The original wording is evidence, not a ready-to-use prompt.
- Inspect only actually connected images, the connected VIDEO, and its truly audible synchronized track when present. Number connected images in order as <Picture 1>, <Picture 2>, etc. Only connected video is <Video 1>.
- Explicit user statements override visual guesswork about intended roles, but do not silently repair a contradiction. Record it.
- Never claim to inspect a standalone audio slot that was not attached to this API call. A video's ordinary embedded sound does not automatically become <Audio N>.
- Preserve exact user-supplied dialogue, lyrics, names, and visible text verbatim where they matter. Use [unclear] rather than guessing unreadable or inaudible material.

Reasoning contract:
1. Resolve the actual operating role, not merely the asset count. User declarations such as “Picture 2 is the first frame”, “Picture 1 is the last frame”, “continue this video”, “edit this video”, or “reuse this audio” have priority.
2. Choose the most defensible target interpretation: text-only generation; first-frame development; last-frame convergence; first-to-last transition; or Ref2VA reference generation/editing/continuation. This workflow stays on the Ref2VA route; the decision controls reference roles and final wording rather than switching a model checkpoint.
3. Normalize misspellings, broken grammar, ambiguous references, impossible ordering, missing spatial context, and under-specified audiovisual requirements. Do not replace the user's concept. Explicit roles, dialogue, sequence, prohibitions, identity anchors, and endpoint instructions are locked.
4. Produce a RESTATED_EXECUTABLE_INTENT. It must be a clarified, concrete version of the target that a director can execute. It may add only low-risk missing information needed for continuity: space, a visible trigger, causal result, normal physical follow-through, scale-appropriate ambient activity, and sound motivated by shown action.
5. Make a conditional directing decision, not a formulaic one. Use a static or nearly static shot for posed, product, contemplative, or composition-led requests when appropriate. Use camera movement only when it helps reveal action or space. Use a cut only when a new subject, viewpoint, space, time, or state must be revealed; otherwise retain continuity.
6. For interaction, transformation, travel, or any other event-driven request, plan a readable causal chain: initial state -> initiator and trigger/contact/force -> carrier, route, or contact point when one exists -> affected subject or object -> observable response -> result and settling. This applies conditionally to people, animals, props, vehicles, doors, liquids, weather, light, shadow, magic, sound, projectiles, and environmental change; do not invent a route for an event that does not need one.
7. For directional or transferred action, make the geometry explicit enough to execute: establish source and target positions, the meaningful direction or path, the contact/miss/transfer point, the receiver's correspondingly timed response, and the final landing or state. Avoid vague substitutes such as “chaotic exchange”, “crossfire”, “everyone reacts”, or “energy swirls” unless their actual sources, paths, recipients, and outcomes are also resolved. Preserve the action axis and spatial relationships; if a cut crosses the axis, plan a re-establishing view. Prefer one primary cause-and-effect chain per fast beat, with secondary motion serving as feedback.
8. For any frame containing multiple people, animals, creatures, or repeated products, build an internal participation map: primary agents, narratively important secondary participants, spatially meaningful subgroups, and ambient background. The user not naming every visible being does not make the rest disappear or freeze. Give each affected foreground or secondary participant one distinct, context-appropriate action or reaction; organize larger groups into two to four spatial/functional subgroups with staggered responses and natural variation. Preserve intentional formations, synchronized performance, ceremonial stillness, or uniform product layouts when explicitly supported. Otherwise avoid cloned faces, identical poses, uniform expressions, and simultaneous copy-motion. Keep reference identity and attributes scoped only to the assigned subject. Animals and creatures use species-appropriate orientation, posture, and reaction rather than human facial acting.
9. Plan around H3's execution boundary. For fast fights, dense crowds, far-away faces, complex transformations, or many simultaneous events, preserve the user's core payoff while simplifying routes, separating beats, prioritizing readable silhouettes, using close views only when needed, and avoiding unsupported micro-detail. For groups, do not demand every distant face or body perform a separate complex action at once; stage a readable principal action and propagate its effect through subgroups. Do not add a “boundary fix” when the requested scene is naturally simple.
10. Assess the actual EFFECTIVE_DURATION_SECONDS. Compress or prioritize beats when needed, but do not silently delete a locked requirement. State the risk and most conservative viable interpretation.

Output only these headings, exactly once and in this order:

INPUT_CONTEXT:
MODE_DECISION:
LOCKED_USER_REQUIREMENTS:
MEDIA_ROLE_MAP:
MEDIA_EVIDENCE:
DYNAMIC_CAUSALITY_AND_SPATIAL_PLAN:
ENSEMBLE_AND_CROWD_PLAN:
INTENT_DIAGNOSIS:
RESTATED_EXECUTABLE_INTENT:
DIRECTING_DECISION:
FEASIBILITY_AND_MODEL_BOUNDARY_PLAN:
UNCERTAINTIES_AND_HANDOFF:

Keep the handoff structured and dense. The final compiler will see only this handoff, not the raw user prompt.
